full_text_en:
Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Kemaoyou Co., Ltd. v. Johnson & Johnson (Shanghai) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. and Johnson & Johnson (China) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. — dispute over vertical monopoly agreement

**Ruling Summary**

An agreement, decision, or other concerted practice that restricts minimum resale prices shall constitute a monopoly agreement only if it has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. The economic effects of a minimum resale price restriction may be comprehensively assessed from four aspects: whether the relevant market is sufficiently competitive, whether the implementing undertaking has a strong market position in the relevant market, whether the implementing undertaking has the motive to restrict competition, and the competitive effects of the minimum resale price restriction.

Plaintiff: Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Kemaoyou Co., Ltd., domiciled at Garden Road, Haidian District, Beijing.
Legal representative: Wang Yingjian, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Defendant: Johnson & Johnson (Shanghai) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., domiciled at Fute West 1st Road, Waigaoqiao Free Trade Zone, Shanghai.
Legal representative: Xie Wenjian, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Defendant: Johnson & Johnson (China) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., domiciled at Nanguzhi Road, Minhang Economic and Technological Development Zone, Shanghai.
Legal representative: Xie Wenjian, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

The plaintiff, Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Kemaoyou Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ruibang Company), filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court against the defendants, Johnson & Johnson (Shanghai) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Johnson & Johnson Shanghai) and Johnson & Johnson (China) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Johnson & Johnson China), concerning a dispute over a vertical monopoly agreement.

**Plaintiff's Allegations**

The plaintiff alleged that, as a distributor of the two defendants' medical staplers and surgical sutures in the Beijing area, it had cooperated with the two defendants for 15 years. In 2008, because it reduced its bid price in a procurement bidding process at Peking University People's Hospital (hereinafter referred to as People's Hospital), in violation of the resale price restriction clause in the distribution contract, it was punished by the two defendants. First, its distribution rights in some hospitals were revoked, and subsequently, its supply was completely cut off, causing substantial economic losses. The acts of the two defendants in stipulating a resale price restriction clause in the distribution contract and, based on that clause, penalizing Ruibang Company up to terminating the distribution contract, constituted the illegal act listed in Article 14, Item (2) of the Anti-Monopoly Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Anti-Monopoly Law), i.e., "restricting the minimum price for resale of commodities to a third party." Therefore, the plaintiff requested, pursuant to Articles 3, 14, and 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, that the two defendants be ordered to compensate the plaintiff for economic losses of RMB 14,399,300 caused by the above illegal acts, and to bear all litigation costs.

**Defendants' Defense**

The two defendants argued that the signing of the distribution contract involved in this case and the alleged monopolistic acts occurred before the implementation of the Anti-Monopoly Law, and therefore the Anti-Monopoly Law should not apply to this case; that the alleged monopoly agreement was jointly signed and executed by both parties, and the plaintiff, Ruibang Company, as a direct participant and implementer of the alleged monopolistic acts, was not qualified to bring this lawsuit; that the economic losses claimed by Ruibang Company were, in nature, losses under a contract dispute and unrelated to the monopoly dispute. Accordingly, the defendants requested that all claims of Ruibang Company be dismissed.

**Facts Found by Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court at First Instance**

The plaintiff, Ruibang Company, was a distributor of the two defendants' staplers and sutures in the Beijing area. The parties had a 15-year cooperative relationship, with distribution contracts renewed annually for a one-year term. On January 2, 2008, the three companies signed the "2008 Distribution Contract" (hereinafter referred to as the "Distribution Contract"), stipulating that the plaintiff would sell suture products in the relevant areas designated by the two defendants, with the contract term from January 1, 2008, to December 31, 2008. Article 2 of Appendix 5 to the contract provided that the plaintiff must not sell at prices lower than those stipulated by the two defendants. On July 1, 2008, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai, on the grounds that the plaintiff had privately reduced the selling price in the bidding at People's Hospital in March 2008, revoked the plaintiff's sales rights at Fuwai Cardiovascular Hospital of the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Beijing Plastic Surgery Hospital (hereinafter respectively referred to as Fuwai Hospital and Plastic Surgery Hospital). Apart from the two defendants, other operators of the above medical suture products included Nantong Hualikang Medical Instruments Co., Ltd., B. Braun Melsungen AG (Germany), Nantong Huaerkang Medical Supplies Co., Ltd., Tyco Healthcare (USA), and Shandong Weigao Group Medical Polymer Products Co., Ltd. Johnson & Johnson Shanghai introduced on the internet the long history of Johnson & Johnson and its suture products, as well as the global market share of its suture products.

**Opinion of Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court at First Instance**

First, according to Article 13, Paragraph 2 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, a monopoly agreement as defined in the Anti-Monopoly Law refers to an agreement, decision, or other concerted practice that excludes or restricts competition. Therefore, to determine whether an act specified in Article 14 of the Anti-Monopoly Law constitutes a monopoly agreement, it is insufficient to rely solely on whether the undertaking and its trading counterpart reached an agreement fixing or restricting resale prices; it is also necessary to further examine whether such an agreement has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. In this case, the evidence submitted by the plaintiff, Ruibang Company, consisted only of a brief introduction by the defendant, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai, on the internet regarding its suture products. This evidence could not precisely reflect the market share of the products in question in the relevant market and could not illustrate the level of competition in the relevant market, product supply, or price changes. On the contrary, the defendants submitted evidence showing the existence of multiple suppliers of similar products. In this case, the factual basis for finding that the defendants engaged in monopolistic conduct was insufficient. Second, the damages caused by monopolistic conduct should primarily be damages arising from the exclusion or restriction of competition. The losses claimed by the plaintiff in this case were all damages that could be claimed in a sales contract dispute and were not directly related to the price restriction clause itself.

In conclusion, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 2 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning Evidence in Civil Litigation and Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, rendered the following judgment on May 18, 2012:

All claims of the plaintiff, Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Kemaoyou Co., Ltd., were dismissed.

Ruibang Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court, alleging: 1. Horizontal monopoly agreements under Article 13 and vertical monopoly agreements under Article 14 of the Anti-Monopoly Law are explicitly prohibited by law because the purpose of the conduct is illegal. Once such agreements are signed, they constitute monopoly agreements, and it is not necessary to further determine whether they have the effect of excluding or restricting competition. 2. The appellees, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai and Johnson & Johnson China, restricted minimum resale prices with the direct aim of restricting competition, which should constitute a monopoly agreement. 3. Pursuant to Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Dispute Cases Arising from Monopolistic Conduct (hereinafter referred to as the Supreme People's Court Monopoly Dispute Trial Provisions), the drafter of an alleged horizontal monopoly agreement bears the burden of proving that the agreement does not have the effect of excluding or restricting competition. By analogy, the appellees, as the drafters of the vertical agreement clauses in this case, should also bear the burden of proving that the agreement in question does not have the effect of excluding or restricting competition. 4. The resale price restriction implemented by the appellees was neither for promoting new products nor for improving product technology, and had no pro-competitive effects at all. On the contrary, the appellees' conduct distorted the market competition mechanism, restricting both intra-brand and inter-brand competition, maintaining the price of Johnson & Johnson suture products in the Beijing area at a very high level, and seriously harming consumer interests. 5. The losses claimed by the appellant all originated from the appellees' illegal implementation of the resale price restriction and were all losses within the meaning of the Anti-Monopoly Law, for which the appellees should compensate. The appellant requested that the first-instance judgment be reversed and that the appellant's first-instance claims be granted.

The appellees, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai and Johnson & Johnson China, argued: 1. According to Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court Monopoly Dispute Trial Provisions, the finding of a horizontal monopoly agreement also requires the element of the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Since vertical agreements have a lesser impact on market competition than horizontal agreements, finding a minimum resale price restriction agreement to constitute a monopoly agreement even more requires the prerequisite of having the effect of excluding or restricting competition. 2. Since there are no special provisions in laws or judicial interpretations, the minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case is not subject to a reversal of the burden of proof. The appellant, Ruibang Company, still bears the burden of proving that the agreement in question has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. 3. The appellant failed to provide evidence demonstrating that the minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case had the effect of excluding or restricting competition. 4. The products in question, medical suture products, were fully competitive in the mainland China market. The agreement in question did not have the effect of excluding or restricting competition; on the contrary, it could enhance competition among Johnson & Johnson brand distributors in areas such as product promotion, after-sales service, brand maintenance, and good faith compliance. 5. The Anti-Monopoly Law came into effect on August 1, 2008. The Distribution Contract in this case was signed in January 2008, and the two appellees' revocation of the appellant's distribution rights at two hospitals occurred in July 2008. After August 1, 2008, the appellees did not implement the monopolistic conduct alleged by the appellant. Therefore, the Anti-Monopoly Law should not apply to this case. 6. The losses claimed by the appellant in this case were not "monopoly losses" but losses resulting from contractual conduct. 7. The Anti-Monopoly Law protects fair market competition order, consumer interests, and public social interests, but does not protect the interests of participants or implementers of monopolistic conduct. Therefore, the subjects entitled to bring an antitrust lawsuit are competitors and consumers who suffer harm from monopolistic conduct, and do not include participants or implementers of monopolistic conduct. Hence, the appellant is not a proper plaintiff in this case. The appellees requested that the appellate court affirm the original judgment.

During the second instance, the appellant, Ruibang Company, clarified that it only alleged that the appellees, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai and Johnson & Johnson China, engaged in monopolistic conduct with respect to medical suture products. Both parties presented evidence on this matter. The appellant submitted nine sets of evidence on five aspects: whether the relevant market in this case should be subdivided into markets for absorbable sutures and non-absorbable sutures; the market share of Johnson & Johnson's suture products in the relevant market; the specific process of the appellant's participation in the People's Hospital bidding; price changes of the products in question; and Johnson & Johnson's management methods for distributors. The appellees submitted two sets of evidence regarding the estimated market share of their suture products in the relevant market. After cross-examination by both parties and certification by the appellate court, the appellate court admitted the appellant's evidence concerning price changes of the products in question and Johnson & Johnson's management methods for distributors, admitted the appellees' submitted "2009 China Health Statistical Yearbook," and did not admit other evidence from either party.

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon hearing the second instance, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

**Additional Facts Found by the Appellate Court in the Second Instance**

1. Regarding the marketing system for the products in question. All Johnson & Johnson products in question were sold through distributors; Johnson & Johnson did not engage in direct sales. Distributors were not permitted to sell competing brands of similar products. Johnson & Johnson authorized distributors on a hospital-by-hospital basis; without authorization, a distributor could not sell in a hospital. For the same brand of suture products, hospitals typically selected only one distributor, usually based on factors such as product price, business dealings, distributor sales service, and hospital payment terms. 2. Regarding the minimum resale price restriction. Prior to 2009, Johnson & Johnson had consistently employed minimum resale price restrictions. After 2009, it revised its distribution agreements and abandoned the long-standing minimum resale price restrictions. 3. Regarding medical suture products. All brands of suture products were required to comply with national suture product standards. In practice, there was no uniform, authoritative, or widely recognized evaluation of the quality of different brands. When choosing between different brands of suture products, hospitals were less sensitive to product prices. However, within the same brand, hospitals tended to select distributors that could offer lower prices. 4. Regarding the market launch time of the products in question. The vast majority of the products in question were registered before 2004, and by 2008 they were no longer new products. 5. Regarding the prices of the products in question. As of 2008, Johnson & Johnson's suture products had maintained basically unchanged prices for 15 years. After the appellant, Ruibang Company, engaged in low-price bidding at People's Hospital, the sales price of the products in question at People's Hospital remained at the appellant's quoted level. 6. Regarding distributor sales services. Distributors' pre-sale services primarily included product promotion, price quotation, and price negotiation. After-sale services primarily included stocking, delivery, regular and ad-hoc visits to hospitals, assisting in answering hospital inquiries, and assisting in collecting clinical usage feedback information.

The appellate court further found: On August 15, 2008, the appellant, Ruibang Company, sent an order for suture products to the appellees. The appellees refused to supply, even though the appellant was not in arrears on payment. Subsequently, the supply of suture products was terminated. After September 11, 2008, the appellees also terminated the supply of stapler products. However, by that time, the appellant had several payments overdue beyond the 30-day credit term, which already met the conditions for termination of supply stipulated in the Distribution Contract.

The issues in dispute in the second instance were: 1. Whether the Anti-Monopoly Law should apply to this case given that part of the conduct of the appellees, Johnson & Johnson Shanghai and Johnson & Johnson China, occurred before the effective date of the Anti-Monopoly Law on August 1, 2008; 2. Whether the appellant, Ruibang Company, as a party to the Distribution Contract and as the signatory and implementer of the minimum resale price restriction clause in this case, had standing as a plaintiff in this action; 3. Whether the effect of excluding or restricting competition is a constituent element for finding a monopoly agreement; 4. How the burden of proof should be allocated regarding the effect of excluding or restricting competition of the agreement in question; 5. Whether the minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case constitutes a monopoly agreement because it excludes or restricts competition; 6. Whether the appellant's claim for damages should be upheld.

**Opinion of the Shanghai High People's Court in the Second Instance**

1. The Anti-Monopoly Law shall apply to this case. The Anti-Monopoly Law came into effect on August 1, 2008. Although the Distribution Contract in this case was signed on January 2, 2008, its validity continued until December 31, 2008. After the Anti-Monopoly Law took effect, the contract was not terminated, and Johnson & Johnson and the distributors continued to perform the contract and implemented the alleged monopolistic conduct. Therefore, the Anti-Monopoly Law shall apply to this case.

2. The appellant, Ruibang Company, is a proper plaintiff in this action. First, a distributor that loses the opportunity to sell below the minimum resale price due to the implementation of a minimum resale price restriction agreement may lose some customers and profits, and thus falls within the scope of civil subjects who suffer losses due to monopolistic conduct as stipulated in Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law. Second, it is usually difficult for interested parties outside the contract to know the specific circumstances of a monopoly agreement. If parties to a monopoly agreement who are privy to the details and possess evidence are not permitted to bring an antitrust lawsuit, such unlawful monopolistic conduct would be difficult to prosecute. Finally, Article 1 of the Supreme People's Court Monopoly Dispute Trial Provisions provides that "civil dispute cases arising from monopolistic conduct as referred to in these Provisions" means "civil litigation cases filed with the People's Court by natural persons, legal persons, or other organizations who have suffered losses due to monopolistic conduct or who have disputes arising from the content of contracts, articles of association of industry associations, etc., violating the Anti-Monopoly Law." The appellant filed this lawsuit because of a dispute with the appellees over whether the content of the Distribution Contract violated the Anti-Monopoly Law, and thus is an plaintiff eligible to file a civil action under that article.

3. A monopoly agreement as specified in Article 14 of the Anti-Monopoly Law must have the effect of excluding or restricting competition as a constituent element. Article 13, Paragraph 2 of the Anti-Monopoly Law provides: "Monopoly agreements as referred to in this Law refer to agreements, decisions, or other concerted practices that exclude or restrict competition." This definition of monopoly agreement applies to the entire Law. Therefore, the vertical agreements specified in Article 14 of the Anti-Monopoly Law must be "agreements that exclude or restrict competition" to constitute monopoly agreements. According to Article 7 of the Supreme People's Court Monopoly Dispute Trial Provisions, finding that a horizontal agreement prohibited under Article 13 of the Anti-Monopoly Law constitutes a monopoly agreement requires the prerequisite that the agreement has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. By implication from the more serious to the less serious (a fortiori), vertical agreements, which have relatively weaker competition-restricting effects, must even more so have the effect of excluding or restricting competition as a necessary condition.

4. The appellant, Ruibang Company, bears the burden of proving that the minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case has the effect of excluding or restricting competition. Since there are no special provisions in the current law or judicial interpretations regarding the burden of proof for minimum resale price restriction agreements, the reversal of the burden of proof does not apply in this case. Pursuant to the principle "he who asserts must prove," the appellant still bears the burden of proving that the minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case excludes or restricts competition.

5. The minimum resale price restriction agreement in this case constitutes a monopoly agreement. This case should be analyzed from the following four aspects: whether the relevant market is sufficiently competitive; whether the defendant's market position is strong; the defendant's motive for implementing the minimum resale price restriction; and the competitive effects of the minimum resale price restriction.

(1) The relevant market in this case is not sufficiently competitive. Insufficient competition in the relevant market should be the primary condition for finding that a minimum resale price restriction agreement constitutes a monopoly agreement. Only when it is determined that the relevant market lacks sufficient competition is it necessary to further assess the competitive effects of the allegedly monopolistic agreement. First, based on the following facts, it can be confirmed that the relevant market in this case is the mainland China market for medical suture products: (a) Medical sutures are essential for wound closure in surgical procedures, and there are currently no other products that can substitute for medical sutures. (b) China imposes strict access restrictions on the production and sale of medical devices, and there is a lack of substitutability between domestic and foreign markets. There is no evidence to suggest that domestic hospitals would choose to purchase suture products from abroad. Therefore, the relevant geographic market in this case should be defined as mainland China. Second, based on the following facts, it can be confirmed that the relevant market in this case is a market with insufficient competition: (a) The cost of purchasing sutures for hospitals can ultimately be passed on to patients. Therefore, the medical suture market lacks sufficient price competition pressure from buyers. (b) Johnson & Johnson promoted suture sales by cultivating and reinforcing the usage habits of doctors and nurses regarding Johnson & Johnson suture products. Doctors and nurses develop brand loyalty to suture products due to their usage habits, which reduces competition in the relevant market. (c) The medical suture product market has multiple high entry barriers, including market access, brand loyalty, and the long-standing and relatively stable customer relationships among suture product manufacturers, distributors, and hospital clients. These barriers make it difficult for potential competitors to enter this market. (d) Johnson & Johnson's suture product prices remained essentially unchanged for 15 years, indicating that Johnson & Johnson has strong pricing power in the relevant market, which can conversely demonstrate that the medical suture market is a market lacking competition.

2. Johnson & Johnson has a strong market position in the relevant market in this case. An enterprise that implements minimum resale price maintenance and has a strong market position in the relevant market, capable of affecting market competition, should be considered as having an important condition for an agreement on minimum resale price maintenance to constitute a monopoly agreement. Based on the following facts, it can be concluded that Johnson & Johnson has a strong market position in the relevant market: (1) According to publicity on Johnson & Johnson's website, its suture products hold a market share of over 70% globally and over 80% in the U.S. market. Johnson & Johnson is capable of providing but fails to provide the exact market share of its suture products in the mainland Chinese market. Considering its litigation position in this case, the actual market share of its suture products in the relevant market should be higher than its estimated market share of approximately 20.4%. Evidence in this case shows that Johnson & Johnson's suture products hold a very high market share in Grade III Class A hospitals in Beijing. (2) The fact that the prices of Johnson & Johnson's suture products have remained essentially unchanged for 15 years and the company has long possessed strong pricing power in the relevant market indicates both that competition in the relevant market is insufficient and that Johnson & Johnson has a strong market position in the relevant market. (3) Johnson & Johnson and its suture products enjoy a high reputation globally and in the Chinese market, and its brand influence has, to a certain extent, maintained its market position in the relevant market in this case. (4) Johnson & Johnson exercises strong control over its distributors; distributors are prohibited from selling other brand products, hospital clients are allocated among distributors by Johnson & Johnson, Johnson & Johnson carries out strict supervision and management over distributors, and the practice of short-term one-year contracts forces distributors to be subject to Johnson & Johnson.

3. The motive for implementing minimum resale price maintenance in this case was to avoid price competition. The motive for minimum resale price maintenance can serve as an important factor in determining whether such conduct has the effect of restricting competition. Evidence in this case demonstrates that Johnson & Johnson implemented minimum resale price maintenance to avoid price competition: (1) Evidence such as the Distribution Agreement and its annexes shows that Johnson & Johnson not only prohibited distributors from proactively lowering prices but also treated passive price reductions under market pressure as grounds for negative evaluation of distributor performance. (2) Evidence submitted by the Appellant, Ruibang Company, regarding distribution management plans shows that when the prices of Johnson & Johnson's suture products were at a competitive disadvantage, Johnson & Johnson preferred to maintain prices through customer relationship management rather than lowering prices.

4. The minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case has a clear restrictive effect on competition, while its pro-competitive effect is not evident. Minimum resale price maintenance can either promote or restrict competition. Only when it actually produces restrictive effects on competition that are difficult to overcome or offset should a minimum resale price maintenance agreement be deemed a monopoly agreement, with special attention paid to effects that substantially impact market competition. First, the minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case has a clear restrictive effect on competition: (1) Johnson & Johnson has enforced minimum resale price maintenance for many years; the prices of its suture products have remained essentially unchanged for 15 years and are generally higher than those of other brands. It can be confirmed that Johnson & Johnson's long-term minimum resale price maintenance practices have helped keep its suture product prices above competitive levels. (2) Johnson & Johnson's conduct has also provided opportunities for other brand manufacturers to avoid price competition, thereby weakening price competition in the relevant market. (3) Johnson & Johnson's conduct has excluded efficient distributors, maintained its pricing system, and thereby harmed consumer welfare. Second, the minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case does not have a clear pro-competitive effect: (1) It is insufficient to prove that the minimum resale price maintenance enhanced product quality and safety, as described by the Appellee. The quality and safety of suture products primarily depend on factory production and medical staff usage. Production quality is ensured by Johnson & Johnson, and training for medical staff is also Johnson & Johnson's responsibility. Regardless of price restrictions, the sales services provided by distributors do not significantly contribute to improving product quality and safety. (2) It is insufficient to prove the necessity of using minimum resale price maintenance to solve the distributor free-riding problem, as described by the Appellee. Hospital clients are allocated among distributors by Johnson & Johnson; without Johnson & Johnson's authorization, even if a distributor lowers prices, it cannot take clients away from other distributors. Thus, no free-riding issue exists. (3) It is insufficient to prove the necessity of using minimum resale price maintenance to facilitate the entry of new brands or new products into the relevant market. This is because Johnson & Johnson's Ethicon suture brand is an established brand, and the products involved are not new products. (4) It is insufficient to prove that the minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case had other economically explainable pro-competitive effects—such as maintaining product reputation, encouraging inventory holding, or expanding the distributor system—from which consumers could benefit.

In summary, the pro-competitive effects of the minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case are not evident or are very limited, and they are far outweighed by its effects of excluding and restricting competition. Therefore, it can be confirmed that the minimum resale price maintenance clauses in the Distribution Agreement in this case constitute a monopoly agreement prohibited by the Anti-Monopoly Law. The Appellee's actions in formulating this agreement and penalizing the Appellant, Ruibang Company, pursuant to this agreement are illegal.

VI. The Appellee shall bear compensation liability for the losses caused to the Appellant, Ruibang Company, by the monopolistic conduct in this case. Pursuant to Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, the Appellee in this case shall bear compensation liability for the losses caused to the Appellant by formulating and implementing the monopoly agreement in this case.

1. Regarding the loss of profit on suture products for 2008 claimed by the Appellant, Ruibang Company. The Appellant asserted that, based on past performance, it could reasonably have been expected to complete its full-year sales target for 2008 under normal circumstances. However, due to the Appellee's cessation of supply, the Appellant failed to complete tax-inclusive sales of RMB 4,704,873.31 for suture products. Calculated at an average gross profit margin of 23%, this resulted in a loss of profit of RMB 1,082,120.86. Upon review: (1) This loss has a direct causal relationship with the Appellee's enforcement of the minimum resale price maintenance agreement in this case. The right on which the Appellant bases its claim for damages originates from the Anti-Monopoly Law and constitutes compensation for losses within the meaning of the Anti-Monopoly Law. (2) In the Appellant's calculation of completed sales for 2008, part of the sales confirmed by the court in another product dispute was omitted. After recalculation, the Appellant's uncompleted tax-inclusive sales of suture products for 2008 should be adjusted to RMB 3,281,910. (3) The Appellant cannot calculate the amount of loss compensation according to the rules of contract law, i.e., it should not calculate losses based on the profits that would have been obtained under the minimum resale price maintenance agreement. Instead, the loss of profit should be calculated by reference to normal profits in the relevant market. After considering factors such as the prices of other brand products in the same industry and the tax burden the Appellant should bear, it is determined that the normal profit the Appellant could have obtained should be approximately equivalent to 16% of the tax-inclusive sales revenue. Accordingly, the normal profit for the Appellant's lost suture product sales in 2008 caused by the Appellee's monopolistic conduct is determined to be RMB 530,000.

2. Regarding other losses claimed by the Appellant, Ruibang Company. The Appellant's other claims for losses are difficult to support: When the Appellee ceased supply of stapler products, the Appellant was already in arrears on multiple payments. The Appellee's cessation of supply of stapler products was in accordance with the terms of the contract. Therefore, the loss of profit on stapler products for 2008 and the price difference loss from purchasing stapler products at a higher price claimed by the Appellant have no direct causal relationship with the monopolistic conduct in this case. The performance bond claimed by the Appellant had already been offset against the outstanding payments in another product dispute. The claimed losses for 2009 lost profits, inventory backlog, employee severance costs, promotional expenses incurred during 15 years of distribution activities, and goodwill damage all lack a direct causal relationship with the monopolistic conduct in this case. Furthermore, there is no legally or contractually expectable interest in these claims, and they are unfounded in law.

In summary, the original judgment was indeed erroneous and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 14, Paragraph 1, Item (2) and Article 50 of the Anti-Monopoly Law, and Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Shanghai High People's Court, on August 1, 2013, rendered the following judgment:

1. The civil judgment of the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court ((2010) Hu Yi Zhong Min Wu (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 169) is reversed;

2. The Appellees, Johnson & Johnson (Shanghai) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd. and Johnson & Johnson (China) Medical Equipment Co., Ltd., shall, within ten days of this judgment taking effect, jointly compensate the Appellant, Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Technology Trade Co., Ltd., for economic losses in the amount of RMB 530,000;

3. The remaining claims of the Appellant, Beijing Ruibang Yonghe Technology Trade Co., Ltd., are dismissed.

This judgment is final.
